content: Do not take any medications, including over-the-counter (OTC) drugs such as antacids, laxatives, or vitamins, without consulting your physician. Before starting dicloxacillin, inform your healthcare provider if you are using any of the following: Tetracyclines: This includes antibiotics like tetracycline, doxycycline, minocycline, omadacycline (Nuzyra), or sarecycline (Seysara). Probenecid: A medication commonly used to treat gout. Warfarin: A blood thinner (brand names include Coumadin and Jantoven). This list may not include all possible drug interactions with dicloxacillin. Always discuss your full medication list with your healthcare provider. Overdose Instructions: If you or someone else has taken too much dicloxacillin, seek immediate medical attention. Call 911 or contact a Poison Control Center at 800-222-1222. Missed Dose Instructions: If you miss a dose of dicloxacillin, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and proceed with your regular dosing schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for the missed one. It is crucial to complete the full prescribed course of dicloxacillin, even if your symptoms improve or resolve, to prevent the development of antibiotic resistance. Uses of Dicloxacillin: Dicloxacillin is an antibiotic used to treat bacterial infections caused by specific bacteria. It is not effective against all infections, as some bacteria may be resistant to it. Dicloxacillin is only effective for bacterial infections and will not work for viral infections such as the common cold, influenza, or COVID-19. Misuse of antibiotics for non-bacterial infections can lead to reduced effectiveness in treating bacterial infections in the future. Your healthcare provider may also prescribe dicloxacillin for other conditions as deemed appropriate. Mechanism of Action: Dicloxacillin works by killing certain bacteria. It does this by inhibiting the bacteria's ability to form a cell wall, which is essential for their survival. Dosage Forms: Dicloxacillin is available in the following oral capsule forms: 250 mg capsules 500 mg capsules Storage Instructions: Store dicloxacillin at room temperature, between 68°F to 77°F (20°C to 25°C). It can tolerate short-term exposure to temperatures between 59°F to 86°F (15°C to 30°C), such as during transportation. How to Use: Dicloxacillin capsules should be swallowed whole. Common Side Effects: The most common side effects of dicloxacillin include: Nausea Vomiting Diarrhea Black, hairy tongue If any of these side effects bother you, inform your healthcare provider. There may be other side effects not listed here. Contact your healthcare provider if you suspect you are experiencing a side effect. You can also report side effects to the FDA at 800-FDA-1088 or Health Canada at 866-234-2345. Serious Side Effects: Although less common, serious side effects of dicloxacillin include: Severe Allergic Reactions: Stop taking dicloxacillin and seek immediate medical attention if you experience: Breathing difficulties or wheezing Rapid heartbeat Fever or general unwellness Swollen lymph nodes Swelling of the face, lips, mouth, tongue, or throat Difficulty swallowing or throat tightness Itching, skin rash, or hives Nausea or vomiting Dizziness, lightheadedness, or fainting Stomach cramps Joint pain Antibiotic-Associated Diarrhea: Dicloxacillin can cause an overgrowth of Clostridioides difficile (C. diff) in the gut, leading to antibiotic-associated diarrhea. This condition can occur even up to two months after stopping the antibiotic. Contact your healthcare provider immediately if you experience: Watery diarrhea Persistent diarrhea Blood in your stool Severe stomach cramps Fever that begins after starting or finishing the medication Seizures: Some individuals taking dicloxacillin have reported seizures. Signs of a seizure include: Muscle twitching, jerking, spasms, tremors, or other uncontrolled movements Stiffening of the arms and legs Anxiety, nervousness, confusion, or a sense of dread Dizziness or lightheadedness Fainting or loss of consciousness Stop taking dicloxacillin and contact your healthcare provider if you experience any of these symptoms. Kidney Damage: Dicloxacillin may cause kidney damage. Notify your healthcare provider immediately if you experience: Decreased urination Swelling in the feet, ankles, or legs Weakness or unusual fatigue Difficulty breathing or chest pain/pressure Confusion Nausea Seizures Blood Disorders: Dicloxacillin can lead to blood disorders such as eosinophilia, hemolytic anemia, agranulocytosis, neutropenia, leukopenia, or bone marrow depression. Stop using dicloxacillin and seek medical attention if you experience: Fever Shortness of breath Pale or yellowish skin Easy bruising or bleeding Frequent infections Unusual weakness or fatigue Dizziness, lightheadedness, or fainting Headache Rapid or irregular heartbeat Liver Damage: Dicloxacillin may cause liver damage (hepatotoxicity). Contact your healthcare provider immediately if you experience: Nausea or vomiting Stomach or abdominal pain Fever Weakness or unusual fatigue Itching Loss of appetite Light-colored stool Dark-colored urine Yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice) Precautions: Who Should Not Use Dicloxacillin: Do not take dicloxacillin if you are allergic to: Dicloxacillin itself Any ingredients in the specific product dispensed (your pharmacist can provide a full list of ingredients) Important Considerations Before Use: Take dicloxacillin on an empty stomach with a large glass of water (at least 4 ounces or 120 milliliters) at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal. Remain sitting or standing upright while taking dicloxacillin. Avoid taking it while lying down or just before bedtime. Only take dicloxacillin if it has been prescribed to you by a healthcare provider. Do not share this medication with others, even if they have the same condition, as it may harm them. Keep dicloxacillin out of reach of children. Inform Your Healthcare Provider: Before starting dicloxacillin, inform your healthcare provider about all your health conditions and any medications, vitamins, minerals, herbal products, or supplements you are taking. This will help determine if dicloxacillin is appropriate for you. Specifically, discuss: Any allergies to penicillin or other medications Asthma Nausea, vomiting, or gastrointestinal issues History of antibiotic-associated diarrhea Kidney problems Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: It is not known if dicloxacillin can harm an unborn baby. Inform your healthcare provider if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Dicloxacillin passes into breast milk. Inform your healthcare provider if you are breastfeeding or planning to breastfeed. Drug Interactions: Food and Drink: Dicloxacillin is best absorbed on an empty stomach. Take it with a large glass of water at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals. The effects of alcohol on dicloxacillin are unknown, but heavy drinking can weaken your immune response and make it harder for your body to fight infections. Other Medications: Always inform your healthcare provider about all prescription and OTC medications, vitamins, minerals, herbal products, and supplements you are taking. Avoid taking additional medications, including OTC drugs like antacids, laxatives, or vitamins, without physician approval. Discuss the following medications specifically: Tetracyclines (e.g., tetracycline, doxycycline, minocycline, omadacycline, sarecycline) Probenecid Warfarin This may not be a complete list of potential interactions. Always consult your healthcare provider for guidance.
